Press Release:


Legalising Medical Marijuana
Government has taken its first official steps in legalising the manufacture of marijuana for medicinal use, mandating the Medicines Control Council to investigate the potential of cannabis’ properties and efficacy in treating terminal illnesses, cancers, conditions causing chronic pain and more. Carte Blanche asks: Where will research into the impact of this enigmatic plant take us?


Script:


LEGALISING MEDICAL MARIJUANA

PRODUCER: ESTE DE KLERK

PRESENTER: BONGANI BINGWA

EDITOR: ROBIN LEUCI

BROADCAST DATE: 26 FEBRUARY 2017

Marijuana – is it the devil we’ve been indoctrinated through ages to believe it is? Or is it the wonder drug many are now attesting to?
Despite anecdotal evidence that medicinal cannabis treats certain ailments and the Medicines Control Council recommendation to Parliament last year that it be legalized for medicinal use, it’s still illegal to use, buy, sell, manufacture and grow cannabis in South Africa.

BONGANI LINK: Cannabis is an illegal substance in South Africa, but increasingly it has been used as the wonder cure for any number of ailments. The dealer has become the healer. But is this dangerous?

Because it’s still an illegal substance, many ill and desperate people are buying it from growers who are manufacturing their own medicinal products.
One such ill and desperate patient, who admitted to using cannabis oil, was terminally ill IFP MP dr Mario Oriani-Ambrosini who introduced the Medical Innovations Bill in 2014, before he passed away. He fought for the legalization of medical cannabis.

South Africa is now one step closer to having the drug legalized and the Medicines Control Council’s policy framework should be published for public comment within the next few weeks, says chairperson Prof Helen Rees.

PROF HELEN REES: It is going to look at everything – from the conditions for growing, the conditions for manufacturing, for packaging, the security conditions, what kind of people should be allowed to be given a permit, because clearly one of the things we want to avoid is that as we develop this as a potential medicine and potential industry, that we don’t want this getting into the wrong hands.

It has been claimed that Cannabis has a profound effect on a variety of conditions because of a network in the human body called the endocannabinoid system, or ECS found in the central nervous and immune systems. The ECS is responsible for a large number of physiological processes in the brain and human body. Our bodies themselves manufacture these cannabinoids, but researchers have identified more than a hundred cannabinoids in the cannabis plant – most well-known for their effects are those called THC and CBD.

Stellenbosch University Physiologist, dr John Lopes has done research on both these cannabinoids, as well as the cannabinoid called HU-210.

DR JOHN LOPES: THC increases your heart rate. CBD will slow down your heart rate, so it is almost as if they have opposing effects and the ratio of this is absolutely essential. Let’s say THC is very high, that will dominate the effect and when you have a high level of CBD, that will dominate the effect.

PROF HELEN REES: So far we have very few studies which would really get us to the point of what we call licensure, that will give us enough hard evidence to show that this indication looks like it is effective and that the product is safe. We need to rapidly move from anecdote into proper clinical trials.

Cannabis has been used medicinally for centuries. Its extracts were widely used by physicians in ancient China, India, Egypt and Europe. It was also popular in the US in the 19th century.

DR BEARMAN: It was found in many medicines, doctors wrote prescriptions for it. As late as the 1920s American physicians wrote three million prescriptions a year that contained cannabis.

But despite its benefits, cannabis was banned in the USA. It was also banned in South Africa in 1928.
In 2013, Uruguay became the first country to legalise medical marijuana, followed by 28 states in the US, and several other countries across the globe.

A Johannesburg medical doctor – who branched out in homeopathy and Chinese Medicine, says she’s been prescribing medicinal cannabis in her practice with good results.

DR “X”: In my practice I found it to be most effective for patients undergoing chemotherapy or radiation to reduce nausea, to increase blood counts, it increases appetite, neuro-pathic pain associated with chemotherapy. It increases a patient’s sense of wellbeing. I know it is effective for insomnia and for anxiety, some types of skin cancers, then we found it to be quite effective for glaucoma as well.

BONGANI TO PROF REES: How concerned are you that for many people cannabis seems to be this cure-all?

PROF REES: People are buying things that might have nothing in them and they could be dangerous. They have no knowledge of what they are buying, if it has got cannabis in it and it is imported, it is illegal. So, people are being exploited and very often the people who are being exploited, are people who are desperate. No doctor worth their salt will recommend it unless they have proper evidence.

DR “X”: Once we’ve done the correct trials, we’ll be able to understand what strain of cannabis works for what condition and we’ll be able to prescribe correctly, whereas now we’re just doing a shot-gun approach.

Ralph Higgo is a supporter of the use of medical cannabis. He says he doesn’t sell any cannabis products.

BONGANI TO RALPH: Being such an advocate for medicinal cannabis, why are you not selling it?

RALPH: I would like a license to sell.

BONGANI TO RALPH: Are you concerned that you would be targeted because you encourage people to use medicinal cannabis?

RALPH: Yes, I worry a lot and it scares me. But in the same breath, this is bigger than me and it’s for an important cause.

Ralph says oversight and standardization are very necessary, but this will unfortunately not kill the illegal trade.

RALPH: But that is still not going to stop the next-door neighbor from growing his own plant and making his dagga tea or his own cannabalm.

PROF HELEN REES: It can’t be just I got a plot in my back garden and then I can grow something and then pulp it up and make an oil. It cannot be like that. It has to be grown in a particular fashion that can be standardize, and you have to be able to extract in standard fashion. You have to be able to preserve it and make it in a formulation so that you know that when you give this for example in a clinical trial, you know exactly how many milligrams you are giving in a dose and that’s how you find out how something works.

A great concern to scientists like dr Lopes, is how the oil is currently extracted from the plant.

DR LOPES: People are using various agents to extract oil – Ethanol is also used in laboratries, methanol sometimes people use. Sometimes people use benzyne. In the end you need to have a pure oil and need to get rid of those agents.

When avid mountaineer, Eldaline Botha heard she had an aggressive carcinoma with only nine months to live, she told her oncologist she would use cannabis oil whilst undergoing chemotherapy. And she says it made all the difference

ELDALINE: I have a cancer with unknown primary, which means we don’t know where it is. To this day we don’t know where it is. Couldn’t operate and remove it.

BONGANI: So, looking at the various treatment options, you told your doctor that you would also be using cannabis?

ELDALINE: I said but I want to use cannabis and he said that is fine, how do you want to use it? And that’s what you discuss with the person who supplies it, how much do I need to take, when do I need to take it? I took high volumes so I can sleep. That helps you, believe it or not, deal with results of chemotherapy.

BONGANI: At the end of your chemo-sessions, what did the doctors say?

ELDALINE: Well, when I got to him the last time he looked at me and said you have a zero count.

BONGANI: Did your doctors recognize the impact of the cannabis along with the treatment they proscribed?

ELDALINE: They clearly had an interest in what was happening if I took the cannabis. I’ve never, not from one of the doctors experience an attitude of don’t use that, it is dangerous.

The MCC has to get its framework ready for public comment and the Medical Innovations Bill is likely to be promulgated, in the second quarter of this year.
Only then can permits be offered to potential growers.
Applicants will undergo strict security clearances.

PROF HELEN REES: If there are products and we can show that there are medicinal implications, it is better to put it into a legal framework so that people can legitimately get it and not like the way it is now.


PROMOS

PROMO 1:10”

DR “X”: I have found Cannabis to be extremely effective. I’ve been using it in my practice for the last five years with very good results.

How far are we in the process of legalising medical cannabis?

PROMO 2: 15”

Marijuana – is it the devil we’ve been indoctrinated to believe it is? Or the wonder drug many are attesting to?
Are we any closer in having medicinal cannabis legalized?

PROF REES: We need to rapidly move from anecdote into proper clinical trials.

PROMO 2:15”

It’s still illegal to grow, manufacture, sell, buy or use medicinal cannabis – yet the illegal trade is booming.
PROF REES: PROF REES: People are buying things that have nothing in them and they could be dangerous. People are exploited and quite often it’s those who are desperate
